title: Rain product choice changes the runoff decline estimate by 13 points at 16 long-record south-east Australian gauges
abstract: We tested whether the small long-record gauge sample explains conflicting accounts of recent runoff change. We fitted the same annual rain-runoff model on 1957-1996 at 16 long-record and 134 other south-east Australian gauges. We compared 2010-2021 with 1985-1996. The planned sample difference was unresolved: SILO changes were -4.0 and -10.6 percentage points of calibration mean flow; their difference was +6.5 (95% spatial-cell interval -6.4 to +13.0). AGCD changes were -16.9 and -15.2 points. An exploratory paired check found that AGCD gave a 12.9-point larger decline than SILO at the same 16 long gauges (interval 2.4-20.7). An exact model decomposition gave -13.54 points from differences in estimated rain change and +0.65 points from fitted slopes. Thus a weak recent change at the long gauges is not robust to rain-product choice. The product-effect difference between samples remains uncertain. Neither product is validated here. The test uses published modern annual data, seven long-sample cells, conditional spatial intervals and an annual linear model. It does not test early historical departures or a physical cause. Code, provenance, results, audits and figures are included.

display.caption: The same 16 long-record gauges show a 4-point runoff residual decline with SILO rain and a 17-point decline with AGCD. Bars show spatial-cell intervals. The paired product check is exploratory.

citations.reason: Published modern annual data and the regional time-pattern question.
Uses long-record gauge membership. Challenges the robustness of a weak recent era contrast to rain product choice; does not retest the century-scale window result.
